title: India's Biggest Trade Deal Goes Live in 17 Days. It Has Deployed 1,000 People to Make Sure Nobody Misses It.
excerpt: The India-UK CETA takes effect on July 15, cutting tariffs on everything from whisky to automobiles. For Indian professionals in Britain, it also means five years of not paying into a pension system they may never use.
body:
In seventeen days, the most comprehensive free trade agreement India has ever signed will come into force. And Delhi is not waiting around.

Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal, speaking at the 10th Annual UK-India Week in London this past week, announced that the government is deploying 1,000 advisory personnel across India to help businesses — including first-time exporters from Tier-2 and Tier-3 cities — understand and use the provisions of the India-UK Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement before it kicks in on July 15.

"The UK Free Trade Agreement is going to be the most comprehensive agreement that India has entered into so far, and it will come into force in July," Goyal said at the India Global Forum's Capital & Future Frontiers Forum.

His British counterpart, Business and Trade Secretary Peter Kyle, framed it as a race. "We are bringing our landmark trade deal with India into force as quickly as we can," Kyle said. The entry-into-force is the fastest turnaround Britain has achieved on any trade agreement it has ever signed.

## What the Numbers Look Like

The bilateral trade relationship between India and the UK is already worth £48 billion a year. The CETA is projected to add another £25.5 billion annually in the long run, while boosting UK GDP by £4.8 billion and real wages by £2.2 billion.

Some of the tariff cuts are dramatic. Indian whisky exporters — an industry that barely existed a decade ago but is now producing globally competitive single malts — will see UK import duties drop from 150 per cent to 40 per cent. Automobile tariffs fall from 100 per cent to 10 per cent under a quota. Cosmetics tariffs of up to 22 per cent will be eliminated either immediately or over ten years.

Going the other way, the UK will cut tariffs on Indian clothes, footwear and certain food products. The deal liberalises 99 per cent of UK tariffs and 90 per cent of Indian tariffs, covering nearly every product category that moves between the two economies.



> **""We are bringing our landmark trade deal with India into force as quickly as we can," Kyle said."**


India has never implemented a deal of this size, which gives the UK what the British government describes as an "immediate competitive advantage" over other markets.

## The Clause That Matters Most to the Diaspora

Buried in the technical provisions of the agreement is a measure that could put thousands of pounds back into the pockets of Indian professionals working in Britain.

Under the India-UK Double Contributions Convention, which enters into force alongside the trade deal, eligible Indian professionals on pre-existing visa routes will receive a five-year exemption from UK social security contributions. Instead of paying into the British National Insurance system — which they might never draw benefits from — these workers can redirect those savings into interest-bearing, tax-free provident fund accounts in India.

The arrangement is reciprocal: British professionals working in India will receive equivalent treatment, continuing to pay National Insurance at home without facing Indian social security deductions. The UK already has similar arrangements with countries like Japan, South Korea and Canada.

For the roughly 900,000 people of Indian heritage living in Britain — many of them in high-skilled professional roles — this is arguably the most tangible personal benefit of the entire agreement.

## The Steel Problem That Nearly Derailed It

The path to July 15 was not smooth. Negotiations over implementation nearly stalled last month when India raised concerns about British steel safeguard measures due to take effect on July 1. Under the UK's proposed measures, tariff-free import quotas on steel would be slashed, and duties on shipments exceeding the quota would nearly double to 50 per cent.

Indian officials suggested aspects of the trade deal could be renegotiated. The steel dispute drew particular attention because India is both a major steel producer and exporter, and the new measures threatened to undercut the goodwill generated by the agreement. There were reports that India considered retaliatory measures, including reducing concessions on Scotch whisky.

Kyle played down the dispute, telling reporters that "the FTA is what it is" and that implementation talks were "going well." But the episode underscored the complexity of translating a signed agreement into a functioning trade architecture.

## From Birmingham to Bengaluru

Goyal highlighted an unusual feature of the delegation he brought to London. Alongside the expected corporate heavyweights were companies from India's smaller cities — first-time exporters who had never attended an international trade event.

The government's upgraded trade portal and 1,000-person advisory network are designed for precisely these businesses. The idea is that the CETA should not just expand existing trade corridors between Mumbai and London, but create new ones — between places like Birmingham and Gujarat, Manchester and Maharashtra.

India is the world's fastest-growing major economy, and Goyal urged Indian companies to adopt international quality standards and position themselves as early movers. "Confidently promote Brand India," he said.

The partnership has evolved far beyond traditional trade, extending into technology, sovereign AI, critical minerals, defence and clean energy. But for most businesses and professionals, the deal's value will be measured in the specifics: the tariff saved, the licence not needed, the contribution not deducted. Those specifics go live on July 15.

*Sources: Devdiscourse, GOV.UK, Reuters, Latestly, The Hindu Business Line*
